title: American's Claim That Aloo Bhujia 'Cured' His Asthma Amuses the Internet
excerpt: A Massachusetts man's viral video crediting simple Indian food — illustrated with a packet of aloo bhujia — for curing his asthma and allergies drew a wave of jokes from Indian netizens, and a reminder that anecdotes aren't medical evidence.
body:
• Samuel Hillclimber, a Massachusetts-based man who posts on Instagram as @cowboymansam, went viral after claiming in a video that eating "simple Indian food" cured his asthma and allergies.
  • The detail that delighted Indian viewers: to illustrate the medicinal power of Indian spices, he held up a packet of aloo bhujia and read out its ingredients — cumin, mango powder, garlic powder, onion powder, lemon powder, turmeric powder, mint leaves.
  • Netizens flooded the comments with jokes: "Be careful, samosa might unlock your chakras too," one wrote; another admitted, "As an Indian, I did not know aloo bhujia cures asthma"; others suggested he try Hyderabadi dum biryani or Chyawanprash next.
  • The medical reality: asthma has no proven food cure, and one person's anecdote is not evidence — dietary changes should never replace prescribed asthma medication without a doctor's guidance.

An American man has gone viral with a bold claim: that eating "simple Indian food" cured his asthma and allergies. Samuel Hillclimber, a Massachusetts-based creator who posts on Instagram as @cowboymansam, shared a video praising Indian food and its spices as "extremely medicinal" — while illustrating his point with a packet of aloo bhujia.

The video

In the video, Samuel reads out the ingredients printed on the snack packet one after another: "Cumin, mango powder, garlic powder, onion powder, lemon powder, turmeric powder, mint leaves." He calls the spices amazing on the stomach and declares: "I cured my asthma and my allergies by using simple Indian food, okay?"

He goes further, suggesting that people managed asthma before modern inhalers ever existed. "You think we didn't have technology to cure asthma before inhalers? We did," he says, according to The Times of India.

The internet responds

The comments section became the real show. "I don't think highly processed packaged food can cure anything brother," one user wrote. "Well... Aloo Bhujia was unexpected," said another. An Indian viewer confessed, "As an Indian, I did not know aloo bhujia cures asthma," while someone else joked that if Samuel tried Chyawanprash — the Ayurvedic herbal jam — he would "become superman." Others nominated his next discovery: "Wait until he discovers Hyderabadi dum biryani." One viewer predicted superhuman powers "after one golgappe."

A few agreed with part of his argument — "I agree most of these spices are medicinal!" — but the dominant tone was affectionate ridicule.

"Be careful, samosa might unlock your chakras too."

— an Instagram commenter

What the science actually says

Spices do have studied properties — turmeric, ginger and garlic all appear in research on inflammation — but there is no clinical evidence that any food cures asthma, and medical guidance is unambiguous that dietary changes should complement, never replace, prescribed asthma medication. Even the original report carried the caveat: Samuel's statements about curing asthma and allergies are his personal claims and should not be taken as medical advice, or as evidence that aloo bhujia or Indian spices can cure these conditions.

Why it traveled

The video's spread says as much about food culture as about health claims. Indian snacks — from bhujia to biryani — have become global comfort food, and the image of an American earnestly reading an aloo bhujia ingredient list as if it were a pharmacopoeia struck a chord with Indian and diaspora audiences alike. The result was less a debate about asthma treatment than a light-hearted conversation about Indian spices, snacks and the strange things that go viral online.
